blocks.text: Either in Scripture itself or in the ancient versions of Scripture, seven kinds of fly are found. I. The fly properly so called, in Hebrew זבוב zebub, in Greek μυῖα [myia], Eccles. X, 1: Dead flies make the perfumer's ointment give off a stench. Esa. VII, 18: The Lord will hiss for the fly that is in the uttermost part of the rivers of Egypt. II. The bee, in Hebrew דברה debora, in Greek μέλιττα [melitta], Deut. I, 44: They chased you, as bees do. Iud. XIV, 8: And behold, a swarm of bees in the body of the lion. Psalm. CXVIII, 12: They surrounded me like bees. Esa. VII, 18: The Lord will hiss for the fly, etc. and for the bee that is in the land of Assyria. III. The wasp or hornet, in Hebrew צרעה tsira, in Greek σφὴξ [sphēx] or σφηκία [sphēkia], as the Greek translators have it, Exod. XXIII, 28: I will send the hornet before you, which will drive out the Hivite, etc. Deut. VII, 20: Moreover the Lord your God will send the hornet among them. Ios. XXIV, 12: I sent the hornet before you, which drove them out from before you. IV. Οἶστρος [oistros], the oestrum or asilus [gadfly]. Alluding to its name, the Greeks say at Ezech. II, 6 Διότι παροιστρήσουσιν [Dioti paroistrēsousin], For, as if stung by the gadfly, they will rage, and at Os. IV, 16 Ὡς δάμαλις παροιστρῶσα παρεῖστρησεν Ἰσραήλ [Hōs damalis paroistrōsa pareistrēsen Israēl]: Like a heifer struck by the gadfly, Israel has raged. V. The κυνόμυια [kynomyia], or dog-fly, is often named in the Greek version. Thus Exod. VIII, 21 Ἰδοὺ, ἐγὼ ἐξαποστέλλω ἐπὶ σὲ κυνόμυιαν [Idou, egō exapostellō epi se kynomyian], and throughout the rest of the chapter; and Psal. LXXVII, 45 Ἐξαπέ- [col. 497] στειλεν εἰς αὐτοὺς κυνόμυιαν [Exapesteilen eis autous kynomyian]; and Psal. CIV, 31 Εἶπε, καὶ ἦλθε κυνόμυια [Eipe, kai ēlthe kynomyia]. But Jerome, at the end of his Letter to Sunnia and Fretela, wants κοινόμυιαν [koinomyian] to be read. For this Aquila has παμμυῖαν [pammyian], because the Hebrew ערב arob is thought to be taken from mixture. Accordingly there are also some among the Hebrews who interpret it so. But of these below, in their proper place. VI. To the kinds of fly may be referred κώνωψ [kōnōps], the gnat, of which Matth. XXIII, 24 Οἱ διυλίζοντες τὸν κώνωπα, τὴν δὲ κάμηλον καταπίνοντες [Hoi diylizontes ton kōnōpa, tēn de kamēlon katapinontes], Straining out the gnat, but swallowing the camel. VII. As also σκνίπες [sknipes] (or, as others read, σκνίφες [skniphes]), Exod. VIII, 16 Ἔσονται σκνίπες ἔν τε τοῖς ἀνθρώποις, καὶ ἐν τοῖς τετράποσι καὶ ἐν πάσῃ γῇ Αἰγύπτου [Esontai sknipes en te tois anthrōpois, kai en tois tetraposi kai en pasē gē Aigyptou]. And Psal. CIV, 31 Καὶ σκνίπες ἐν πᾶσι τοῖς ὁρίοις αὐτῶν [Kai sknipes en pasi tois horiois autōn]. The Vulgate translator too and Jerome have sciniphes. But Josephus and the more recent Hebrews more correctly render the Hebrew כנים as lice. Now we shall speak of the fly properly so called.

The fly, as in Hebrew זבוב zebub, so in Chaldee is called דבובא debuba, in Syriac ܕܒܒܐ debaba, and in Arabic ذباب [dhubāb] dsebab, with slight change. The origin of the name, unknown to the Hebrews and Syrians, is disclosed by the Arabs, among whom ذب [dhabba] dsabba means to wander about with no fixed abode and not to stay in one place. That this suits the fly, there is no one who does not know. [III, 342] Hence Lucian in the Encomium of the Fly: Νεοττιὰν δὲ, ἢ καλίαν, οὐχ᾽ ἑνὶ τόπῳ κατεστήσατο, ἀλλὰ πλάνητα τὴν πτῆσιν κατὰ τοὺς Σκύθας ἐπανῃρημένη, ὅπου ἂν τύχῃ ὑπὸ τῆς νυκτὸς καταληφθεῖσα, ἐκεῖ καὶ ἑστίαν καὶ εὐνὴν ποιεῖται [Neottian de, ē kalian, ouch' heni topō katestēsato, alla planēta tēn ptēsin kata tous Skythas epanērēmenē, hopou an tychē hypo tēs nyktos katalēphtheisa, ekei kai hestian kai eunēn poieitai]: She does not establish a nest or a little nest in one place, but, borne up in wandering flight after the manner of the Scythians, wherever she happens to be overtaken by night, there she makes her home and her bed. To the same point belongs the fact that one who is extremely fickle and inconstant is said in an Arabic proverb to be اطيَش من ذباب [aṭyash min dhubāb], more inconstant than a fly ^{(1)}.
